# LDDMM

An R package for Longitudinal Drift-Diffusion Mixed Models (LDDMM), v1.0.0.

**Authors**: [Giorgio Paulon](https://giorgiopaulon.github.io/), [Abhra Sarkar](https://abhrastat.github.io/)

### Overview

Codes accompanying "Bayesian Semiparametric Longitudinal Drift-Diffusion Mixed Models for Tone Learning in Adults" by Paulon, Llanos, Chandrasekaran, Sarkar.

This package implements a novel generic framework for longitudinal functional mixed models that allows automated assessment of an associated predictor's local time-varying influence. We build on this to develop a novel inverse-Gaussian drift-diffusion mixed model for multi-alternative decision-making processes in longitudinal settings. Our proposed model and associated computational machinery make use of B-spline mixtures, hidden Markov models (HMM) and factorial hidden Markov models (fHMM), locally informed Hamming ball samplers etc. to address statistical challenges.

The main function is `LDDMM`; please see the following vignette for details, as well as the main article:

Paulon, G., Llanos, F., Chandrasekaran, B., Sarkar, A. (2021). [Bayesian semiparametric longitudinal drift-diffusion mixed models for tone learning in adults](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2020.1801448). Journal of the American Statistical Association **116**, 1114-1127

The data included in this package was analyzed in: 

Roark, C. L., Paulon, G., Sarkar, A., Chandrasekaran, B. (2021). [Comparing perceptual category learning across modalities in the same individuals](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-021-01878-0). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review **28**, 898-909

and is available [here](https://osf.io/msnq2/).

### Installation

To install the package in R, first install the `devtools` package, and then use the commands
```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(devtools)
install_github('giorgiopaulon/lddmm')
```
If you are using a Windows machine, you might have to also install and configure `Rtools` using the following [instructions](https://CRAN.R-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/).

### Usage

The main function is `LDDMM()`. The data are one row per trial with the
participant, the training block, the input stimulus `s`, the decision `d`, the
response time and a censoring indicator. For numerical stability, most response
times should lie in $[0, 10]$; response times in seconds work well (the bundled
data are in seconds).

```{r setup-usage, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(lddmm)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))

data('data')
head(data)
plot_accuracy(data)
```

#### Fitting the model

The run below is short so that the example is quick; for an analysis use
something like `Niter = 5000, burnin = 2000, thin = 5`.

```{r fit}
set.seed(123)
fit <- LDDMM(data = data,
             hypers = list(s_sigma_mu = 0.1, s_sigma_b = 0.1),
             Niter = 1000, burnin = 500, thin = 2,
             save_z = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
```

#### Population curves

Posterior means and 90% credible bands of the drifts $\mu_{d,s}(t)$ and the
boundaries $b_{d,s}(t)$. Panels are input stimuli, colours are decisions; the
curve with $d = s$ is the correct response.

```{r curves}
plot_post_pars(data, fit, par = 'drift')
plot_post_pars(data, fit, par = 'boundary')
```

#### Posterior predictive checks

For every saved draw, the fit simulates one response of every participant to
every stimulus in every block. `plot_predictive()` compares these simulated
responses with the data: the proportion of each decision, and the 10%, 50%
and 90% quantiles of the response times.

```{r predictive}
plot_predictive(data, fit, type = 'response')
plot_predictive(data, fit, type = 'rt')
```

#### Convergence

Trace plots of the smoothness and variance parameters and of the population
curves should fluctuate around a stable level, and the Metropolis-Hastings
acceptance rates (stored in the fit) should be roughly between 0.2 and 0.6.
Co-clustering probabilities of curves that are only beginning to separate are
estimated with more Monte Carlo error than the curves themselves, so for those
it is worth running two or more chains with different seeds and comparing.

```{r traces}
traces <- data.frame(draw = seq_along(fit$sigma2_1_mu),
                     sigma2_1_mu = fit$sigma2_1_mu,
                     sigma2_mu_ua = fit$sigma2_mu_ua,
                     drift_block1 = fit$post_mean_mu[1, 1, 1, ],
                     boundary_block1 = fit$post_mean_b[1, 1, 1, ])
ggplot(tidyr::pivot_longer(traces, -draw), aes(draw, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = 'free_y')
round(sapply(fit$acceptance, mean), 2)
```

#### Results

`extract_post_mean()` and `extract_post_draws()` return the subject-level
parameters; `compute_WAIC()` compares models. With `save_z = TRUE`, the cluster
labels give the posterior probability that two curves coincide.

```{r results}
head(extract_post_mean(data, fit, par = 'drift'))
compute_WAIC(fit)
# probability that the correct-response curves of the two stimuli share a
# cluster, for each spline coefficient
round(apply(fit$Z[1, 1, , ] == fit$Z[2, 2, , ], 1, mean), 2)
```

#### Model options

Using the article notation, the drift of decision $d$ for input stimulus $s$ is
$\mu_{d,s}^{(i)}(t) = \exp\{f_{\mu,d,s}(t) + u_{\mu}^{(i)}(t)\}$, and the boundary is
$b_{d,s}^{(i)}(t) = \exp\{f_{b,d,s}(t) + u_{b}^{(i)}(t)\}$.
By default (`random_effects = "correct-incorrect"`) every participant has one random effect curve
$u_C^{(i)}(t)$ for correct responses ($d = s$) and one $u_I^{(i)}(t)$ for incorrect responses,
as in the article; `random_effects = "shared"` uses a single curve for both.
The boundary model is selected with the `boundaries` argument of `LDDMM()`:

* `boundaries = "flexible"` (default): $f_{b,d,s}(t)$ varies over time and is locally clustered together with the drifts
* `boundaries = "constant"`: constant boundaries over time, $b_{d,s}^{(i)} = \exp(b_{d,s} + u_{b}^{(i)})$
* `boundaries = "fixed"`: boundaries that vary over time but not across input stimuli, $b_{d,s}^{(i)}(t) = \exp\{f_{b,d}(t) + u_{b}^{(i)}(t)\}$
* `boundaries = "fixed-constant"`: fixed *and* constant boundaries, $b_{d,s}^{(i)} = \exp(b_{d} + u_{b}^{(i)})$

For the constant models the boundary random effects are scalars rather than curves.
Use `cluster = FALSE` to give every input-response combination its own curve,
and `z_max` to change the maximum number of clusters at each block.

#### Worked examples

Two scripts installed with the package walk through a complete analysis:

* `toy_example.R` fits the bundled data and adds subject-level curves,
  co-clustering probabilities, posterior predictive checks, trace plots and a
  model comparison;
* `toy_simulation.R` simulates data from the model's likelihood with known
  parameters, including a tone that is "anti-learned" (it is answered with
  another category more and more often), fits the model and compares every part
  of the posterior with the truth.

```{r examples, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(system.file("examples", "toy_example.R", package = "lddmm"))
file.edit(system.file("examples", "toy_simulation.R", package = "lddmm"))
```

Version 1.0.0 introduces an improved sampler; see `NEWS.md`.
